newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages trapped by uncompromising sides.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages trapped by uncompromising sides.

text.p: The 74 VIP hostages at the centre of Peru's protracted hostage crisis remained caught between the uncompromising postures of the Peruvian government and their Marxist guerrilla captors on Friday.

While President Alberto Fujimori replaced top captives in government posts, the jungle-trained rebels boasted they could stand the harsh conditions inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence even if their prisoners could not.
Despondency gripped Lima on the 17th day of the drama as New Year's hope of a prompt solution faded amid indications the siege would drag on for weeks.
"Unfortunately, that hope has proved an illusion and the positions of both sides have hardened," Peruvian diplomat Antonio Belaunde wrote in an article.

Fujimori on Thursday removed from their posts two police generals captured by the guerrillas -- the head of Peru's anti-terrorism force and the chief of national security. He also swore in a new Supreme Court president to replace the country's top judge held inside the diplomatic residence.

The security chiefs were under fire for the embarrassing lapse that allowed members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) to storm a December 17 cocktail party marking the birthday of Japanese Emperor Akihito and seize 500 VIP hostages.
Some commentators said Fujimori reduced the value of the hostages to their captors by replacing them and sigalling that the country's affairs went on despite the standoff.
The guerrillas also sent a cold message to the outside world insisting they could easily hold out "as long as it takes" but would not guarantee the same for the hostages.

"The guerrillas can stand it -- they've been trained in the jungle. But can the hostages?" MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco said in an interview from Germany. "If they suffer, the Peruvian government must accept all responsibility for not facilitating a solution to this situation."
The remaining captives included Fujimori's brother, two ambassadors, top Peruvian government and security force officials, and Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
The guerrillas were holding those men as bargaining chips to press their principal demand for the release of roughly 400 comrades jailed in Peru.
That tough position was unlikely to have been assuaged by a speech by Fujimori on Thursday in which he condemned the rebels as "terrorists" bent on pointless violence.

He also attacked the MRTA's claim to be fighting for the poor. "It is a crass error to think that the violence that arises from discontent can end poverty," he said. "Twelve years of violence from Shining Path (guerrillas) and the MRTA...has, on the contrary, made us poorer."
But Fujimori gave no clue as to his next move.

Fujimori has kept government negotiator Domingo Palermo away from the residence despite MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa's assurance -- during an impromptu press conference within the building -- that "the doors are open."

Opposition legislator Harold Forsyth proposed that former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, a diplomatic trouble-shooter and peace broker, step in to mediate an end to the crisis. There was no immediate response from the government to the proposal.
The most recent "hostage" to walk free from the residence was a German shepherd dog called Emma.
Looking dejected and emaciated after 16 days without food, the sandy-coloured dog was enticed on Thursday from the diplomatic compound by firemen who offered her Christmas cake.
